As a rapidly developing nation, Malaysia is navigating a complex demographic transition shaped by declining fertility, increased longevity, urbanization, and internal migration. These trends carry significant implications for labor markets, social protection systems, and intergenerational solidarity. Malaysia therefore recognizes that timely, technology-driven, and evidence-based policy responses are essential to ensure that demographic change.

Supports rather than constrains sustainable development.

Malaysia is committed to strengthening its national population data ecosystems by integrating census, survey, and administrative data with robust geospatial information to support evidence-based policy making. The Department of Statistics Malaysia has progressively incorporated geocoding in the 2020 census and precise location-based data for the 2026 economic census, aligning with the global statistical geospatial framework. To further advance these efforts, Malaysia is currently developing a digital-first, multi-mode combined census model for the upcoming 2030 census, leveraging the experience of the Central Database Hub and collaborations with the National Registration Department and Ministry of Health to accelerate the integration of administrative data with geo-AI and artificial intelligence. At the same time, we are modernizing data dissemination through integrated national portals and interactive dashboards to promote transparency, quality, and public trust. Malaysia undertakes regular demographic, social, economic, and behavioral studies to inform policies and programs. close collaboration with universities and research institutions strengthens methodological rigor and policy relevance. Surveys such as the Malaysia Population and Family Survey, the National Health and Morbidity Survey, and the Malaysia Aging and Retirement Survey provide critical insights into fertility trends, health outcomes, and population aging. Complementing these efforts, the Malaysia Population Research Hub, was established to consolidate the demographic research, survey findings and policy-relevant publications to support evidence-based planning. Digitalization of primary healthcare has been accelerated through cloud-based systems and the Health Information Exchange platform, enabling electronic lifetime health records that ensure continuity of care from infancy to old age. These innovations also strengthen monitoring of maternal health and early childhood development. Investments in gerontechnology and artificial intelligence further support healthy ageing and independent living for older persons. Resilience and address social challenges through community-based engagement. Malaysia is also proactively addressing population aging through integrated life cycle-based frameworks. Madam Chair, Excellencies, and distinguished delegates, at the outset, I would like to thank you and members of the Bureau for your leadership in guiding the work of the 59th session of the Commission on Population and Development. Mongolia welcomes the convening of the session and appreciate its focus on population, technology, and research in the context of sustainable development. We believe this is both timely and necessary as technology and better data are increasingly shaping how countries understand demographic change and respond to the people's need. The ICPD program of action remains as relevant today as ever and continues to provide an important framework for advancing sustainable development in a balanced, inclusive, and people-centered manner. As a geographically vast country with dispersed population, Mongolia places particular importance on equitable access to health, education, and social services, especially for women, children, young people, and rural communities. Madam Chair, Mongolia believes that digital transformation can be a practical accelerator of sustainable development. Since its launch in October 2020, the eMongolia platform has delivered 63 million services, reached 1.9 million users, and integrated 1,263 services from 87 government agencies. It has reduced the average time needed to obtain a government service from two and a half hours to about five minutes, generating substantial savings in time, travel, and administrative cost for citizens. These results show how digital public infrastructure can reduce inequalities in access and bring the public service closer to the people. This progress reflects Mongolia's broader digital-first agenda. As highlighted in the report before this commission, Mongolia has achieved internet access in all villages and towns. This is particularly significant for geographically dispersed country such as ours, as improved connectivity helps expand access to information, services, and opportunities for people living in remote and rural areas. Its impact is especially evident in health sector. Through eMongolia platform, citizens can increasingly book appointments, seek consultations, and access medical records and test results online. For families living far from urban centers, digital access to health information and services can make a meaningful difference in continuity of care and timely decision making. In addition, Mongolia recognized that the technology alone is not enough. Its benefits must be supported by stronger health systems and sustained investment in human capacity. In this regard, recent policy measures further demonstrate Mongolia's commitment to strengthening health system. In July 2025, the Ministry of Health approved Mongolia's first Midwifery Development Action Plan 2030, which aims to reduce preventable maternal and newborn deaths, expand access to family planning, and strengthen midwifery nationwide. The government of Mongolia has also announced 2027 as the year of health promotion in order to advance healthy Mongolian objective under the government's 2024 to 28 action program and further strengthen the public health system. Mongolia is also promoting the research-based development of traditional Mongolian medicine. In January 2026, the President of Mongolia, His Excellency Khurleksukh Khokhna, issued a decree to advance traditional Mongolian medicine through improved legal and service framework, stronger training, deeper research on traditional knowledge and its compatibility with modern medicine, and innovation using advanced technology, big data, and artificial intelligence. We see this as a part of broader effort to promote culturally responsive people-centered and knowledge-based health policy while preserving an important element of national heritage. At the same time, Mongolia recognized that technological advancement must be accompanied by strong safeguards. Innovation should be inclusive, ethical, and grounded in human rights. We therefore attach particular importance to strengthening privacy protection, responsible data governance, and public trust in the use of emerging technologies and population data. Madam Chair, Mongolia reaffirms our strong commitment to the full and effective implementation of the ICPT Programme of Action. Thank you very much.
